---
title: "A Web Crawler That Does Not Overload One Host"
description: "Advanced interview case: derive the principle, prove assumptions, and run small code."
---

## Interview challenge

Build a crawler over a billion URLs. You have a large worker fleet, but one site must not receive ten thousand simultaneous fetches merely because it has ten thousand discovered pages. How can the crawler stay fast **and** polite?

A global FIFO queue cannot enforce per-host pacing by itself. The key abstraction is a **frontier with scheduling constraints**.

## Model host-level eligibility

For every host $h$, track the earliest next legal dispatch time $t_h$. A URL at host $h$ may be claimed at time $t$ only if $t\geq t_h$. After dispatch, update $t_h=t+\Delta_h$, where $\Delta_h$ is the site's configured interval.

$$
\operatorname{eligible}(u,t)\iff t\geq t_{\operatorname{host}(u)}.
$$

Other hosts remain eligible even when one host is cooling down. Thus one slow or restricted host need not block the entire frontier.

## Original minimal code

~~~ts
const frontier = new PoliteFrontier();
frontier.enqueue('https://one.example/a');
frontier.enqueue('https://one.example/b');
frontier.enqueue('https://two.example/c');
frontier.claim(0,1000); // one.example/a
frontier.claim(0,1000); // two.example/c
frontier.claim(500,1000); // no eligible URL
~~~

POST /lab/crawl enqueues a URL; GET /lab/crawl/next?nowMs=0&delayMs=1000 simulates dispatch. The unit test checks that one host's rate limit does not prevent another from making progress.

## Why the code intentionally never fetches URLs

A secure crawler must implement **robots.txt**, site policies, response size caps, content types, redirects and DNS/network restrictions that block SSRF to private or metadata endpoints. The teaching code stops at scheduling so it can be executed safely without contacting external sites.

Real crawlers also deduplicate normalised URLs and content hashes, persist visited state, recover unfinished leases and support distributed ownership of each host's pacing state.

## The difficult part with multiple workers

If each worker keeps an independent next-allowed timestamp, two workers may fetch from the same host simultaneously. Make host scheduling ownership explicit: partition by host, or atomically claim a host lease in a shared store. A mere queue partition on URL hashes is insufficient because URLs of one host may end up on many workers.

## Follow-up interview questions

- How should a domain with one million discovered links compete with ten small domains? Use per-host fair queues and global capacity admission.
- What happens on DNS changes or redirects? Recheck targets against SSRF policies and destination-host pacing.
- How would you crawl freshness-sensitive pages without recrawling everything? Add a change-rate model and scheduled revisits.

## Mathematical Abstraction

$$
t_{h,j+1}-t_{h,j}\geq\Delta_h,
\qquad \sum_h\lambda_h\leq C.
$$

The first inequality is the host politeness spacing constraint; the second limits aggregate request rate by crawler capacity $C$. These constraints are independent and both must be satisfied.
